newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: France reluctantly endorses Annan for UN chief.
newsitem.headline: France reluctantly endorses Annan for UN chief.

text.p: France, deploring once again that a U.S. veto prevented the re-election of U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, reluctantly fell in behind U.S.-backed Ghanaian Kofi Annan to succeed him on Friday.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette hinted to reporters at a European Union summit in Dublin that France may have sought the number two job at the United Nations in return for dropping its blocking opposition to Annan in Friday's indicative vote.
France, one of the five permanent Security Council powers with the right to veto candidates, was the last of the 15 Council members to hold out against Annan in test votes this week.

Asked whether Paris wanted the deputy secretary-general job for a Frenchman, de Charette said: "We made known to Mr Kofi Annan our support, we reminded him what our concerns were, in particular our attachment to bilingualism, not only in the person of the secretary-general but also in the practice and daily life and the work of the United Nations."
"We added that we wanted France and Francophone countries to have their fair share of responsibility in the echelons of the U.N. and, it goes without saying, in the secretariat."
De Charette said France had had doubts about Annan's ability to reform the United Nations vigorously after having spent so many years at the centre of the organisation.
But he said the Ghanaian's credentials when he ran U.N. peacekeeping operations and his managerial skills, as well as his fluent command of French, had overcome those misgivings.

Asked whether the election left France with a bitter taste, the minister said: "We profoundly regret the circumstances which led to making Boutros Boutros-Ghali's re-election impossible when it had seemed natural and self-evident a year ago."

President Jacques Chirac telephoned Boutros-Ghali from Dublin to pay tribute to his action in reforming the United Nations over the last five years and express his "personal friendship and solidarity", French spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said.
